bullets: ‘like a child: yet not so like a child as like an old man’: paradox of memory.
‘a bright clear jet of light’: truth; Scrooge later forces the extinguisher cap down on it.
The Ghost’s gentle method: questions and silence; it lets Scrooge see and feel.
Scrooge sees the countryside of his childhood: ‘a thousand odours… long, long, forgotten!’: senses unlock memory.
‘a solitary child, neglected by his friends, is left there still’: pathos.
He remembers reading Ali Baba and Robinson Crusoe: imagination as escape.
He wishes he had given something to the boy singing a carol at his door: first regret, linked to the present.
Fezziwig’s ball: generosity, joy and community; Scrooge defends him to the Ghost and then thinks of Bob: a second regret.
Belle: ‘Another idol has displaced me… a golden one’; ‘You fear the world too much’.
Belle’s later family life: Scrooge sees what he lost; ‘Spirit! remove me from this place.’
He struggles with the Ghost and extinguishes its light: suppressing painful truth.

callouts.p: It explains rather than excuses: Scrooge was lonely and once loved, but he chose money over love. The reader’s sympathy grows alongside Scrooge’s regret.

model: Wish about the carol singer: regret
exam.q: Explore how Dickens presents Scrooge’s feelings in this extract (Stave 2, the schoolroom). (20 marks)
exam.tip: Track the moments Scrooge reacts: they show the change beginning.

mistakes.r: It explains him, but Belle shows he made choices.

summary: Stave 2 extracts focus on the Ghost of Christmas Past, the lonely schoolboy, Fan, Fezziwig’s ball and Belle; learn how Dickens evokes sympathy and regret and plants the first signs of change. (See also the separate notes on Fezziwig, Belle and Fan.)
